bibl.title: Oscillatory patterns in temporal lobe reveal context reinstatement during memory search
bibl.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether the gradually drifting neural state present while a word is studied returns when that word is recalled, and returns with it the states of its list neighbours
span.quote: We sought to determine whether context reinstatement may be observed in electrical signals recorded from the human brain during episodic recall.

span.label: is there direct neurophysiological evidence for contextual reinstatement, which behavioural work has only supported indirectly
span.quote: Although this behavioral evidence provides indirect support for context-based theories of memory, there is no direct neurophysiological evidence for contextual reinstatement.

span.label: finds a neural signature of temporal context reinstatement — recall-time activity resembles study-time activity for the recalled item and, in graded fashion, for its neighbours — and shows its strength predicts each patient's behavioural contiguity effect
span.quote: Upon recalling a studied item, we found that the recorded patterns of brain activity were not only similar to the patterns observed when the item was studied, but were also similar to the patterns observed during study of neighboring list items, with similarity decreasing reliably with positional distance.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Analyzing electrocorticographic recordings taken as 69 neurosurgical patients studied and recalled lists of words, we uncovered a neural signature of context reinstatement.

span.label: temporal context reinstatement during memory search
span.quote: We sought to determine whether context reinstatement may be observed in electrical signals recorded from the human brain during episodic recall.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: To test the context reinstatement hypothesis, we studied 69 neurosurgical patients who were implanted with subdural electrode arrays and depth electrodes during treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Recalling an item revives the contextual state bound to it at study, and that retrieved context then cues other items encoded in similar contexts, which is what produces the contiguity effect.
span.quote: This retrieved context, in turn, activates other memories that were associated with similar contexts, producing the contiguity effect seen in recall tasks ( Fig. 4 B ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A slowly drifting contextual state becomes associated with each event as it is experienced, so that later recall of the event reinstates that state.
span.quote: These theories posit that a gradually changing contextual state becomes associated with each experienced event, and that recalling an event revives the contextual state associated with the original experience.

span.label: context is operationalised by a property the theory predicts — slow drift — so the features analysed are exactly those that could carry a context signal
span.quote: we selected PCA-derived features from study events that showed significant positive autocorrelations ( Materials and Methods ), a defining feature of temporal context, for further analysis

span.label: the circularity that would create is blocked by splitting selection from test: the filter is fitted on study events only, and the hypothesis is tested on recall events
span.quote: To prevent selection bias, recall events were not used in the feature selection process.

span.label: the filter's cost is stated rather than hidden — removing content information also removes the forward asymmetry the behavioural effect shows, so a known feature of the phenomenon is invisible by construction
span.quote: In this way, if our feature selection framework filters out content information, one would not expect to see asymmetry in the neural data (further discussion is provided in SI Materials and Methods ).

span.label: the discriminating prediction is bidirectional decay: content reinstatement alone predicts a forward boost, autocorrelated noise predicts no lag structure, and only context predicts symmetric decay
span.quote: Of these three simulations, only the context reinstatement model predicts that neural similarity will decrease substantially with absolute lag in both the positive and negative directions, as observed in the neural data (further details and discussion are provided in SI Materials and Methods ).

span.label: rival accounts are built and run rather than argued against — three neural network simulations using the same presented and recalled items as the real analysis
span.quote: Each simulation used the same presented and recalled items that were included in our data analyses ( Fig. 4 ).

span.label: the rehearsal alternative is tested through a consequence it would have elsewhere: if rehearsal drove the effect, neural contiguity should track the primacy effect, and it does not
span.quote: Thus, if our basic findings were driven by rehearsal, one might expect that participants exhibiting strong neural contiguity should also show a strong primacy effect. We observed no significant correlation between primacy and neural contiguity ( r = 0.13, P = 0.42; SI Materials and Methods, Analysis Methods and Fig. S2 ), suggesting that rehearsal during study, per se, is unlikely to account for our findings.

span.label: individual differences carry the inference: the same patients supply both the neural measure and the behavioural one, so the two can be correlated across people rather than compared as group means
span.quote: Consistent with the hypothesis that the contiguity effect arises due to context reinstatement ( 5 , 6 , 24 ), participants with stronger neural signatures of context reinstatement exhibited more pronounced contiguity effects than did participants with weaker reinstatement effects ( r = 0.42, P = 0.007; Fig. 4 C ).

span.label: a gradual-drift result is treated as insufficient on its own, because ordinary autocorrelated processes would produce it too
span.quote: Whereas this gradually changing neural representation is consistent with context-based models, such a result would also be expected to arise as a result of other autocorrelated neural processes that lack the rich dynamics implied by context-based theories of memory.

span.label: only negative lags are used for the reinstatement measure, because forward lags cannot separate content from context
span.quote: (Only the regressions for negative lags were used, because the regressions for positive lags are not expected to distinguish between content and context reinstatement; Fig. 3 ).

span.label: the inclusion threshold is justified as an explicit trade-off between dimensionality and sample size rather than presented as a natural cutoff
span.quote: This threshold was chosen to balance two factors. First, we wanted to ensure that the feature vectors were of high enough dimensionality that it would be possible to observe neural signatures of context reinstatement ( Fig. 4 A ) for each participant. Second, we wanted to maximize the amount of data included in our analysis.

span.label: Parietal and occipital results were inconclusive because of insufficient data.
span.quote: Our findings in the parietal and occipital lobes were inconclusive due to insufficient data.

span.label: Null results outside temporal lobe do not establish that other regions are uninvolved.
span.quote: Our inability to find neural signatures of context reinstatement in extratemporal brain regions does not necessarily mean that those regions are not involved in context reinstatement.

span.label: The analysis cannot resolve structures within the coarse regions of interest.
span.quote: Furthermore, our analysis does not distinguish between structures contained within the regions of interest we examined.

span.label: A large share of recording sessions was discarded for having too few candidate context features.
span.quote: We further excluded an additional 68 sessions in which fewer than five candidate context features were identified.

span.label: a null in other regions is not read as evidence of absence
span.quote: Our inability to find neural signatures of context reinstatement in extratemporal brain regions does not necessarily mean that those regions are not involved in context reinstatement.

span.label: the regions of interest are too coarse to identify a structure
span.quote: Furthermore, our analysis does not distinguish between structures contained within the regions of interest we examined.

span.label: two of the four regions could not be assessed
span.quote: Our findings in the parietal and occipital lobes were inconclusive due to insufficient data.

span.label: substantial attrition: features were found in 132 of 144 sessions, then 68 further sessions were dropped for having fewer than five
span.quote: Features that met these criteria were identified in 132 (of 144) recording sessions. We further excluded an additional 68 sessions in which fewer than five candidate context features were identified.

span.label: rehearsal-based and context-based accounts are conceded to be hard to tell apart in principle
span.quote: Rehearsal-based models have been shown to be difficult to distinguish from context-based models ( 34 , 35 ), likely because a context-based mechanism is necessary to explain the pattern of rehearsals made in a free-recall task.

span.label: the primacy control rests on rehearsal being the mechanism of primacy, which the paper acknowledges is not settled
span.quote: Although rehearsal is one of the hypothesized mechanisms underlying primacy, we recognize that other factors, such as enhanced attention to early list items ( 39 , 41 ), may also contribute to primacy.

span.label: electrode placement was set by clinical need, not by the hypothesis
span.quote: The clinical team determined the placement of these electrodes with the goal of localizing suspected epileptogenic foci and identifying functional regions to be avoided in surgery

span.label: principal components analysis and the Kaiser criterion, used to turn thousands of correlated frequency-electrode measurements into a small orthogonal basis in which event-to-event similarity is preserved
span.quote: In this way, each component reflects a linear combination of the power in each frequency band across all recording electrodes, such that the pairwise neural similarities between events are preserved.

span.label: a 20-neuron simulated network, used not to model the brain but to derive what each competing account would predict for the lag profile
span.quote: Pattern of activations for a simulated 20-neuron neural network as a 15-item list is studied.

span.label: the Hilbert transform on band-passed signals, with power computed across the whole session before segmentation specifically to avoid edge artifacts
span.quote: To reduce edge artifacts, we computed power at each frequency for the entire recording session before parsing the recordings into experimental events.

span.label: Rehearsal-based models → context-based models
span.note: THE TWO CANNOT BE SEPARATED IN THIS STUDY - the DESIGN form (Q-286/Q-287). It bounds what the paper's own results can mean, and it lives in a methods paragraph where nothing downstream will find it. TWO MODEL CLASSES THAT CANNOT BE TOLD APART BY THE DATA, with the reason given: a context-based mechanism is needed to explain the rehearsal pattern, so the two are entangled by construction.
span.quote: Rehearsal-based models have been shown to be difficult to distinguish from context-based models ( 34 , 35 ), likely because a context-based mechanism is necessary to explain the pattern of rehearsals made in a free-recall task.

span.label: context — as external environmental conditions versus as an internal, ever-changing mental state; the paper's theory requires both
span.quote: the reinstatement of a gradually changing context representation that reflects not only external conditions, but also an ever-changing internal context state ( 1 , 2 )

span.label: context — operationalised: the principal components whose activity is positively autocorrelated during study, and nothing else
span.quote: In the remainder of this paper, we refer to the set of autocorrelated principal components as feature vectors.

span.label: reinstatement — of content (the item's own representation) versus of context (the states of its neighbours); the whole design exists to separate these
span.quote: To distinguish between content and context reinstatement, we compared the feature vectors associated with each recall event with the feature vectors associated with the neighbors of the recalled word in the study sequence.

span.label: contiguity effect — behavioural (transitions between neighbouring items at recall) versus neural (similarity declining with absolute lag); the paper coins the second and correlates the two
span.quote: Furthermore, the strength of this neural contiguity effect tracks the behavioral contiguity effect in free recall: Participants who exhibit a stronger tendency to make transitions among neighboring items during recall also exhibit a stronger relation between neural similarity and absolute lag.

span.label: contextual features — as environmental cues, as recently studied items, as internal mental states, or as a process evolving randomly; four readings the founding theories left open
span.quote: These contextual features may reflect environmental cues, recently studied items, participants’ internal mental states, or may evolve randomly over time.

span.label: gradual change — as evidence for context versus as the signature of any autocorrelated process; the paper insists the first requires more than the second
span.quote: Whereas this gradually changing neural representation is consistent with context-based models, such a result would also be expected to arise as a result of other autocorrelated neural processes that lack the rich dynamics implied by context-based theories of memory.

span.label: builds-on → retrieved context theories of episodic memory (refs 1, 5, 6, 24)
span.quote: This pattern of results is exactly what one would predict on the basis of retrieved context theories of episodic memory ( 1 , 5 , 6 , 24 ).

span.label: builds-on → Tulving (ref 2) - episodic retrieval as mental time travel
span.quote: This notion is consistent with the contention of Tulving ( 2 ) that episodic memory retrieval is like mental time travel, in that when we remember the past, many details of the prior experience are retrieved along with the desired material.

span.label: supports → retrieved context theories of episodic memory (refs 1, 5, 6, 24), by supplying the neurophysiological evidence they lacked
span.quote: This pattern of results is exactly what one would predict on the basis of retrieved context theories of episodic memory ( 1 , 5 , 6 , 24 ).

span.label: extends → prior demonstrations that an item's own representation is reinstated at recall (refs 25, 26), by showing the neighbours' representations return too
span.quote: In recalling a list item, people not only reinstate that item's representation, as has been recently documented ( 25 , 26 ), but they also revive the brain activity associated with neighboring items.

span.label: contradicts → theories deriving contiguity from direct item-to-item associations formed within seconds (refs 11–14)
span.quote: This result is difficult to explain according to the view that contiguity arises from direct item-to-item associations that are established within a few seconds, as suggested by other classes of psychological and neurobiological theories ( 11 – 14 ).

span.label: critiques → rehearsal-based accounts of the neural contiguity effect, via the absent primacy correlation
span.quote: Nonetheless, it is clear that the mechanisms underlying the primacy effect are unrelated to the neural contiguity effect we observe.

span.label: supports → Tulving's characterisation of episodic retrieval as mental time travel
span.quote: This notion is consistent with the contention of Tulving ( 2 ) that episodic memory retrieval is like mental time travel, in that when we remember the past, many details of the prior experience are retrieved along with the desired material.

span.label: builds-on → the hypothesis that medial temporal lobe and prefrontal cortex maintain and update temporal context
span.quote: For example, recent work has given rise to the hypothesis that the medial temporal lobe ( 23 , 27 – 32 ) and prefrontal cortex ( 22 , 32 , 33 ) are critically involved in the maintenance and updating of temporal context.

span.label: context reinstatement —causes→ contiguity effect
span.quote: Recent neurocomputational models of episodic memory ( 5 , 6 ) suggest that contextual reinstatement underlies the contiguity effect: people's tendency to successively recall items that were presented in nearby positions on a studied list ( 7 ).

span.label: contiguity effect —is-a→ temporal clustering
span.quote: The contiguity effect is an example of temporal clustering, which is perhaps the dominant form of organization in free recall.

span.label: episodic memory —contrasted-with→ semantic memory
span.quote: The pivotal distinction between memory for facts (semantic memory) and memory for episodes or experiences (episodic memory) has been argued to reflect, at least in part, the reinstatement of a gradually changing context representation that reflects not only external conditions, but also an ever-changing internal context state ( 1 , 2 ).

span.label: content reinstatement —distinct-from→ context reinstatement
span.quote: To distinguish between content and context reinstatement, we compared the feature vectors associated with each recall event with the feature vectors associated with the neighbors of the recalled word in the study sequence.

span.label: temporal context —operationalised-as→ autocorrelation
span.quote: we selected PCA-derived features from study events that showed significant positive autocorrelations ( Materials and Methods ), a defining feature of temporal context, for further analysis

span.label: temporal context —operationalised-as→ feature vectors
span.quote: In the remainder of this paper, we refer to the set of autocorrelated principal components as feature vectors.

span.label: context reinstatement —operationalised-as→ neural similarity
span.quote: we calculated the similarity between the feature vector associated with the recall event and the feature vectors associated with each of the studied items (e.g., ant , tape , nose , vase , sheep ), where similarity is defined as the normalized dot product between the feature vectors (the vectors were normalized to have unit length before the dot product was performed)

span.label: rehearsal-based models —contrasted-with→ retrieved context theories
span.quote: Rehearsal-based models have been shown to be difficult to distinguish from context-based models ( 34 , 35 ), likely because a context-based mechanism is necessary to explain the pattern of rehearsals made in a free-recall task.

span.label: autocorrelated noise —contrasted-with→ context reinstatement
span.quote: Of these three simulations, only the context reinstatement model predicts that neural similarity will decrease substantially with absolute lag in both the positive and negative directions, as observed in the neural data (further details and discussion are provided in SI Materials and Methods ).

span.label: free recall —contrasted-with→ cued recall
span.quote: A number of laboratory memory tasks rely on episodic memory, including experimenter-cued tasks (e.g., item recognition and cued recall) and self-cued tasks (e.g., free recall).

span.label: medial temporal lobe —part-of→ temporal lobe
span.quote: temporal lobe (including the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe), frontal lobe (including prefrontal cortex), parietal lobe, and occipital lobe

span.label: rehearsal-based models —operationalised-as→ primacy effect
span.quote: It has been well established that rehearsal is associated with enhanced recall for early list items [i.e., the primacy effect ( 36 – 40 )].

span.label: regression
span.quote: For each participant, we regressed the mean neural similarity between feature vectors on lag separately for positive and negative lags (two regressions were performed for each participant).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: We found that the mean neural similarity at lag = 0 was significantly greater than the mean neural similarity at other lags [paired-sample t test across 39 participants with at least 5 autocorrelated features: t (38) = 3.10, P = 0.004; Fig. 4 A ].

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The similarity in recorded activity during each pair of word presentations decreased with the positional distance between the presentations [ t test on distribution of t values from the regressions: t (68) = −9.31, P < 10 −10 ], indicating that the ECoG recordings evolve gradually over the course of the studied lists.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Consistent with the hypothesis that the contiguity effect arises due to context reinstatement ( 5 , 6 , 24 ), participants with stronger neural signatures of context reinstatement exhibited more pronounced contiguity effects than did participants with weaker reinstatement effects ( r = 0.42, P = 0.007; Fig. 4 C ).

span.label: principal components analysis
span.quote: We then used principal components analysis (PCA) to distill these highly correlated neural features into a smaller number of orthogonal components ( Fig. 1 C ).

span.label: Kaiser criterion for component retention
span.quote: We used the Kaiser criterion to choose, for each participant, the principal components that explained a substantial proportion of the variance ( 44 ).

span.label: autocorrelation
span.quote: We select those components that show significant positive autocorrelation (a defining feature of temporal context) during the study phase of the experiment.

span.label: z-score standardisation
span.quote: Before applying PCA to the frequency × electrode matrices ( Fig. 1 B ), we z -transformed power values relative to the distribution of all events in the recording session (the z -transformation was performed independently for each frequency-electrode pair).

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Error bars in A and B denote ±1 SEM.

span.label: t test
span.quote: t test on distribution of t values from the regressions: t (68) = −9.31, P < 10 −10

span.label: paired-sample t test
span.quote: paired-sample t test across 39 participants with at least 5 autocorrelated features: t (38) = 3.10, P = 0.004

span.label: β coefficient
span.quote: Each regression yielded a t value associated with the slope (β coefficient) of the fitted line.

span.label: principal components analysis
span.quote: We then used principal components analysis (PCA) to distill these highly correlated neural features into a smaller number of orthogonal components

span.label: Kaiser criterion
span.quote: We used the Kaiser criterion to choose, for each participant, the principal components that explained a substantial proportion of the variance ( 44 ).

span.label: z -transformed
span.quote: we z -transformed power values relative to the distribution of all events in the recording session (the z -transformation was performed independently for each frequency-electrode pair)

span.label: SEM
span.quote: Error bars denote ±1 SEM.

span.label: normalized dot product
span.quote: We then compute the similarity (normalized dot product) between the feature vectors of each recall event (e.g., “nose”) and the feature vectors associated with the corresponding study event (lag = 0), as well as the similarity of the recall event to surrounding study events with varying lags.

span.label: Neural similarity between pairs of studied words fell off as the distance between their serial positions grew, showing that the ECoG signal drifts gradually across a list.
span.quote: The similarity in recorded activity during each pair of word presentations decreased with the positional distance between the presentations [ t test on distribution of t values from the regressions: t (68) = −9.31, P < 10 −10 ], indicating that the ECoG recordings evolve gradually over the course of the studied lists.

span.label: Brain activity recorded just before a word was recalled was more similar to activity during study of that same word than to activity during study of any other list word.
span.quote: We found that the mean neural similarity at lag = 0 was significantly greater than the mean neural similarity at other lags [paired-sample t test across 39 participants with at least 5 autocorrelated features: t (38) = 3.10, P = 0.004; Fig. 4 A ].

span.label: Similarity between recall activity and study activity declined with absolute lag in both the forward and backward directions, the pattern predicted by context reinstatement rather than item-content reinstatement.
span.quote: Consistent with the context-reinstatement hypothesis, t tests on the distributions of t values across participants indicated that similarity decreased with absolute lag in both the positive [ t (38) = −3.63, P = 0.0008] and negative [ t (38) = −2.42, P = 0.02] directions ( Fig. 4 A ).

span.label: Participants whose neural reinstatement effect was stronger also recalled neighbouring list items successively more often, linking the neural signature to the behavioural contiguity effect.
span.quote: Consistent with the hypothesis that the contiguity effect arises due to context reinstatement ( 5 , 6 , 24 ), participants with stronger neural signatures of context reinstatement exhibited more pronounced contiguity effects than did participants with weaker reinstatement effects ( r = 0.42, P = 0.007; Fig. 4 C ).

span.label: Restricting the analysis to temporal lobe electrodes still produced the graded decrease of similarity with lag in both directions.
span.quote: We found that neural activity recorded from temporal lobe electrodes exhibited a decrease in similarity with increasing absolute lag in both the positive and negative directions [positive: t (20) = −2.20, P = 0.04; negative: t (20) = −2.82, P = 0.01; Fig. 5 B ].

span.label: The frontal-lobe reinstatement signature showed no relationship to how strongly participants clustered their recalls in time, unlike the temporal-lobe signature.
span.quote: However, this frontal signature of context reinstatement was not correlated with temporal clustering of participants’ recalls ( r = −0.08, P = 0.73).

span.label: Primacy strength was unrelated to neural contiguity, arguing against rehearsal during study as the source of the reinstatement effect.
span.quote: We observed no significant correlation between primacy and neural contiguity ( r = 0.13, P = 0.42; SI Materials and Methods, Analysis Methods and Fig. S2 ), suggesting that rehearsal during study, per se, is unlikely to account for our findings.

span.label: The forward asymmetry that characterises behavioural contiguity was absent from the neural similarity data and from the context-reinstatement simulation.
span.quote: However, the forward asymmetry in the contiguity effect ( Fig. 4 B ) is evident in neither the neural data ( Fig. 4 A ) nor our simulation of context reinstatement ( Fig. 3 F ).

span.label: Among the autocorrelated-noise, content-reinstatement and context-reinstatement simulations, only the context-reinstatement network reproduced the observed symmetric decline of similarity with lag.
span.quote: Of these three simulations, only the context reinstatement model predicts that neural similarity will decrease substantially with absolute lag in both the positive and negative directions, as observed in the neural data

span.label: neural similarity between two study events fell with the positional distance between them, so the recording drifts gradually across a list
span.quote: decreased with the positional distance between the presentations [ t test on distribution of t values from the regressions: t (68) = −9.31, P < 10 −10 ], indicating that the ECoG recordings evolve gradually over the course of the studied lists

span.label: recall-time activity was most similar to study of the same word, at lag zero
span.quote: We found that the mean neural similarity at lag = 0 was significantly greater than the mean neural similarity at other lags [paired-sample t test across 39 participants with at least 5 autocorrelated features: t (38) = 3.10, P = 0.004; Fig. 4 A ]

span.label: similarity also declined with absolute lag in both directions — the signature that separates context from content
span.quote: Consistent with the context-reinstatement hypothesis, t tests on the distributions of t values across participants indicated that similarity decreased with absolute lag in both the positive [ t (38) = −3.63, P = 0.0008] and negative [ t (38) = −2.42, P = 0.02] directions ( Fig. 4 A ).

span.label: patients with a stronger neural reinstatement signature showed a stronger behavioural contiguity effect
span.quote: participants with stronger neural signatures of context reinstatement exhibited more pronounced contiguity effects than did participants with weaker reinstatement effects ( r = 0.42, P = 0.007; Fig. 4 C )

span.label: temporal lobe electrodes showed the bidirectional lag decay, and the effect there tracked behavioural clustering
span.quote: As in the whole-brain analysis, the neural signature of context reinstatement in the temporal lobe was significantly correlated with the temporal clustering of participants’ recalls ( r = 0.48, P = 0.03; Fig. 5 C ).

span.label: the frontal lobe signature did not track behavioural clustering
span.quote: However, this frontal signature of context reinstatement was not correlated with temporal clustering of participants’ recalls ( r = −0.08, P = 0.73).

span.label: neural contiguity did not correlate with the primacy effect, arguing against a rehearsal account
span.quote: We observed no significant correlation between primacy and neural contiguity ( r = 0.13, P = 0.42; SI Materials and Methods, Analysis Methods and Fig. S2 ), suggesting that rehearsal during study, per se, is unlikely to account for our findings.

span.label: the forward asymmetry of the behavioural contiguity effect was absent from the neural data and from the context simulation alike
span.quote: However, the forward asymmetry in the contiguity effect ( Fig. 4 B ) is evident in neither the neural data ( Fig. 4 A ) nor our simulation of context reinstatement ( Fig. 3 F ).

span.label: only the context reinstatement simulation reproduced bidirectional decay; noise and content models did not
span.quote: Of these three simulations, only the context reinstatement model predicts that neural similarity will decrease substantially with absolute lag in both the positive and negative directions, as observed in the neural data (further details and discussion are provided in SI Materials and Methods ).

span.label: participants recalled 22.7% of studied words, with about a third of all responses being repetitions or intrusions
span.quote: Participants recalled 22.7 ± 1.0% (mean ± SEM) of the studied words. Repetitions and incorrect recalls (32.4 ± 2.6% of all responses) were excluded from our analyses, as were responses that occurred within 1 s of a prior vocalization.

span.label: of temporal lobe electrodes, 13.9% were in hippocampus and 27.0% in other medial temporal structures
span.quote: Of the temporal lobe electrodes, 13.9% were located in hippocampus, 27.0% were located in medial temporal lobe structures (excluding hippocampus), and the remaining 59.1% were located in other temporal lobe regions.

span.label: contiguity effect
span.quote: Recent neurocomputational models of episodic memory ( 5 , 6 ) suggest that contextual reinstatement underlies the contiguity effect: people's tendency to successively recall items that were presented in nearby positions on a studied list ( 7 ).

span.label: feature vectors
span.quote: In the remainder of this paper, we refer to the set of autocorrelated principal components as feature vectors.

span.label: lag
span.quote: We assigned each studied item a lag (positional distance) relative to the recalled item (e.g., vase has a lag of +1 to “nose”, ant has a lag of −2 to “nose”, and nose has a lag of 0 to “nose”).

span.label: context (for a target event)
span.quote: The events surrounding a target event, and the thoughts they evoke, may be considered to represent a context for the target event, helping to distinguish that event from similar events experienced at different times.

span.label: temporal clustering score
span.quote: The temporal clustering score measures the degree to which responses were clustered on the basis of their temporal contiguity at study ( SI Materials and Methods, Analysis Methods ).

span.label: context
span.quote: The events surrounding a target event, and the thoughts they evoke, may be considered to represent a context for the target event, helping to distinguish that event from similar events experienced at different times.

span.label: contiguity effect
span.quote: the contiguity effect: people's tendency to successively recall items that were presented in nearby positions on a studied list

span.label: lag
span.quote: We assigned each studied item a lag (positional distance) relative to the recalled item

span.label: similarity
span.quote: where similarity is defined as the normalized dot product between the feature vectors (the vectors were normalized to have unit length before the dot product was performed)

span.label: feature vectors
span.quote: In the remainder of this paper, we refer to the set of autocorrelated principal components as feature vectors.

span.label: temporal clustering score
span.quote: The temporal clustering score measures the degree to which responses were clustered on the basis of their temporal contiguity at study

span.label: context representation
span.quote: context representations are composed of many features that fluctuate from moment to moment, gradually drifting through a multidimensional feature space

span.label: lag (positional distance between a recalled item and a studied item)
span.term: lag (positional distance between a recalled item and a studied item)
span.quote: For each participant, we regressed the mean neural similarity between feature vectors on lag separately for positive and negative lags (two regressions were performed for each participant).

span.label: neural similarity between feature vectors (normalized dot product)
span.term: neural similarity between feature vectors (normalized dot product)
span.quote: For each participant, we regressed the mean neural similarity between feature vectors on lag separately for positive and negative lags (two regressions were performed for each participant).

span.label: oscillatory power in five frequency bands at each electrode
span.term: oscillatory power in five frequency bands at each electrode
span.quote: We constructed a matrix containing, for each electrode, measurements of mean oscillatory power in five frequency bands (δ: 2–4 Hz, θ: 4–8 Hz, α: 8–12 Hz, β: 12–30 Hz, and γ: 30–99 Hz) during each study event (200–1,600 ms relative to each word's appearance on screen) and recall event (−600 to 200 ms relative to vocalization).

span.label: temporal clustering score of recall transitions
span.term: temporal clustering score of recall transitions
span.quote: The temporal clustering score measures the degree to which responses were clustered on the basis of their temporal contiguity at study ( SI Materials and Methods, Analysis Methods ).

span.label: word presentation duration (fixed at 1,600 ms for every item)
span.term: word presentation duration (fixed at 1,600 ms for every item)
span.quote: Following a fixation cue, the computer displayed each word for 1,600 ms, followed by an 800- to 1,200-ms blank interstimulus interval.

span.label: 18-s arithmetic distractor interposed between study and recall on every list
span.term: 18-s arithmetic distractor interposed between study and recall on every list
span.quote: For 18 s following list presentation, participants solved a series of single-digit addition problems of the form A + B + C = X.

span.label: lag
span.quote: We assigned each studied item a lag (positional distance) relative to the recalled item

span.label: neural similarity
span.quote: Mean neural similarity is shown as a function of study distance (difference in serial position) between pairs of presented words.

span.label: mean oscillatory power
span.quote: measurements of mean oscillatory power in five frequency bands

span.label: serial position
